newsitem.title: USA: U.S. considering more food aid to N. Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. considering more food aid to N. Korea.

text.p: In another sign of quickening diplomacy, the United States said on Tuesday it was mulling more food aid to North Korea and that Pyongyang has agreed to hold a second round of talks with Washington on foreign missile sales.

The twin gestures came as Washington and ally South Korea await a formal response from Pyongyang to their proposal for landmark four-party negotiations on a peace treaty for the Korean peninsula. China would also participate.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters the adminstration is "seriously reviewing" the latest appeal made last week by the U.N. World Food Programme for an extra $95.5 million to help North Korea cope with serious food shortages.

The United States responded positively to all previous urgent appeals by the U.N. agency, contributing some $18.4 million for North Korean aid since the fall of 1995, including a $10 million donation now being shipped to Pyongyang.

"Now the United States has not made a formal decision about additional food assistance to North Korea. However, we remain open to appeals by the United Nations humanitarian agencies, and we are seriously reviewing this expanded request by the World Food Programme," Burns said.
He noted Monday's announcement by U.S. grain giant Cargill Corporation of an agreement with North Korea for a rare commercial sale of wheat to the isolated Stalinist regime.

The United States gave Cargill a license in January to sell up to 500,000 tonnes commodities to North Korea. But Burns called the deal "modest" and in Seoul traders close to the deal said North Korea agreed to barter about 4,000 tonnes of zinc for about 20,000 tonnes of wheat.
"We hope very much that there can be efforts to meet the severe food needs of the North Koreans," Burns said.
After an initial reluctance to provide significant amounts of food aid to North Korea, the United States and other countries have shown greater willingness to contribute.
The World Food Programme and visitors to North Korea have provided increasingly compelling accounts of the depth of the crisis there.
A U.S. congressman just back from North Korea said in Tokyo on Tuesday he saw soldiers whose uniforms hung off their bodies, showing that even Pyongyang's elite military was suffering.
"North Korea is rapidly descending into a hell of severe famine," U.S. Representative Tony Hall, a Democrat from Ohio, told reporters after returning from a four-day tour of North Korea.

As for the missile talks, Burns said the North Koreans, who last met U.S. officials on Friday in New York, had "indicated to us their willingness to hold a second round of missile talks very soon." A date and time are being discussed.

The United States has made clear its concern over Pyongyang's missile sales to Iran and Syria and said progress on this issue was critical to improved U.S.-North Korean ties. The first round of missile talks took place in April 1996.

Joseph Bermudez of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank, has called North Korea an "unstable wildcard" in the Middle East that sold short-range missiles to Iran and Syria, ballistic missile technology to Iran, Syria and Egypt and discussed intermediate-range missiles with Iran, Syria, Libya and possibly Egypt.

The United States views the four-party peace talks as a way of reducing tensions on the Korean peninsula -- divided since the 1950-53 Korean War -- and bringing North Korea more into the world community.

U.S. officials say they expect North Korea to arrange a meeting soon at which Pyongyang would deliver its formal response to the four-party talks proposal. There have been rumours Pyongyang has sought another "briefing" on the proposal but U.S. officials deny this.
